                                         Figure 1. Overview and example outputs of SAGE. Given an open-ended user request, our system autonomously composes realistic, diverse,
                                         and simulation-ready 3D environments. The generated scenes are directly deployable in modern simulators, supporting embodied tasks such
                                         as Mobile Manipulation and Pick-and-Place. Through agent-driven reasoning, generator orchestration, and multi-level augmentation, the
                                         framework produces interactive environments at scale for robot policy learning.

    To effectively support embodied AI, simulated data must                                   work for scalable 3D scene generation that produces
satisfy four desiderata: (i) Realism: the geometry, appear-                                   simulation-ready environments directly from arbitrary user
ance, semantic structure, and physics of the simulation                                       prompts. The agent, operating over Model Context Proto-
should resemble the real world closely enough that poli-                                      cal (MCP) [31], adaptively orchestrates generators for floor
cies learned in simulation can reliably transfer to reality;                                  plans, structured layouts, and text-to-3D assets, while two
(ii) Diversity: simulation should encompass a wide range of                                   complementary critics provide continuous feedback: a visual
assets, environments, and tasks to prevent overfitting and sup-                               critic for semantic/spatial coherence and a physics critic with
port generalization; (iii) Simulation-readiness: objects and                                  simulator-in-the-loop validation (Isaac Sim [34]) for stability
scenes must be physically stable, interactable, and directly                                  under gravity and collisions. This closed loop enables self-
compatible with modern simulators for large-scale training;                                   correction without hard-coded tool order and yields scenes
(iv) Task-awareness: simulation environments should adapt                                     that are both realistic and interactable.
to and facilitate the training of various targeted embodied
tasks. For instance, a data engine should provide various                                         We scale these scenes for embodied AI by applying multi-
kitchens for household robots, fire-hazard scenes for rescue                                  level augmentation (object configuration, object category,
robots, surgical rooms for medical robots, etc.                                               and layout) to generate diverse yet task-consistent environ-

Figure 2. Overview of SAGE scene generation. Our system converts open-vocabulary text prompts into simulation-ready 3D scenes by
orchestrating multiple generator tools and critics. The agent dynamically calls generators (Scene Init, Asset Placer/Mover/Remover) to
construct and refine layouts, while visual and physics critics provide iterative feedback for self-improvement. The visual critic suggests
semantic corrections (e.g., missing or misplaced objects), and the physics critic validates stability via Isaac Sim. For example, after applying
physics critic in the bottom image, the newly added pillows on the bed fall flat. This self-improvement process ends when the agent considers
that the generated scene meets the input user requirements. The resulting scenes can be further scaled via augmentation and used for
embodied policy learning.

3.2. Scaling the Scene for Embodied AI                                   embodied AI tasks. We demonstrate their utility on two
                                                                         representative tasks, i.e., Pick-and-Place and Mobile Manip-
To train a robust and generalizable policy, it is not sufficient         ulation, and automatically generate large-scale action demon-
to use a single generated scene; instead, we must generate a             strations using established motion planning techniques. This
diverse set of simulation-ready scenes that follow the user’s            enables scalable policy learning and highlights the benefits
task specification. To this end, we introduce a scene augmen-            of simulation-ready scene generation.
tation strategy that systematically expands each generated
environment into numerous variants while preserving task se-             Pick-and-Place For grasping actions, we use M2T2 [65]
mantics. These augmented scenes are then used to generate                to generate grasp pose candidates from rendered depth im-
corresponding robot actions via motion planning, followed                ages. Collision-free trajectories are computed by integrating
by imitation learning to train task-specific embodied policies.          Curobo [44] into the motion planning and inverse kinematics
                                                                         pipeline, ensuring feasible and stable grasp execution.
3.2.1. Scene Augmentation
To scale one generated scene into a diverse yet task-                    Mobile Manipulation This task is composed of navigation
consistent set of variants, we apply (1) task-relevant ob-               with object pick-and-place in between. For the navigation
ject augmentation (configuration, category) that diversifies             motions, we adopt RRT [21] for robot path planning, gener-
key objects while preserving task semantics, and (2) task-               ating collision-free trajectories between designated start and
irrelevant scene augmentation to enrich the rest of the scenes.          target positions.
                                                                         Failure Modes Motion planning is not always successful,
Object Configuration-level The pose of each task-                        often due to inaccurate grasp pose predictions, unreachable
relevant object (e.g., the target to be picked, placed on, or            target configurations, or unexpected collisions during trajec-
navigated toward) is resampled within the current scene to               tory execution. We filter out failed examples by performing
create variations in object placement. This process increases            collision checks and verifying whether each manipulated
spatial diversity while preserving overall scene semantics.              object reaches its expected location.

                                                                              4.2. Embodied AI Learning
                                                                              We evaluate whether the diversity of our generated scenes
                                                                              enables effective scaling by measuring policy improvements
                                                                              under increasing scene and demonstration counts.

Figure 11. Examples and scaling curve on Mobile Manipulation. Left: task overview. Mid-top: diverse generation. Mid-bottom: example
trajectory. Right: success rate w.r.t. demo/scene counts. Both baselines omit physics critic and replace text-to-3D object synthesis with
retrieval: Baseline 1 mimics SceneWeaver [63]; Baseline 2 further replaces the agent with a fixed pipeline, resembling Holodeck [62].
Diverse SAGE-augmented scenes boost the learned policy’s success and close the gap to the privileged agent, while removing physics critic
and object synthesis degrades performance (Baseline 1). Replacing the agent with a static pipeline further reduces success rate (Baseline 2).

                                                                    17
B.3. Robot Action Generation
Pick-and-Place We use M2T2 [65] to generate grasp pose
candidates from rendered depth images. These are then
transformed using the camera pose to obtain the actual 3D
grasp pose in world coordinates for motion planning with
inverse kinematics (IK). Curobo [44] is integrated into the
motion planning and IK pipeline by incorporating mesh
geometries into its collision checking, ensuring feasible and
stable grasp execution. Once we have the grasp pose, we
divide the grasp into multiple steps. First, we use IK to
calculate the end-effector trajectory from the start pose to
a position directly above the grasp pose. Next, the gripper
lowers and closes to grasp the object. Finally, the gripper lifts
to raise the object. For placement, we use IK with Curobo
collision avoidance. We simplify placement to a drop, which
could be improved with additional motion planning steps to
gently place the object down.

Mobile Manipulation This task is composed of a few
subtasks including object grasping, navigation, and place-
ment. Object grasping follows the same motion planning as
Pick-and-Place. For navigation, we use RRT [21] to plan
collision-free trajectories. The algorithm explores possible
paths from both start and target positions, ending when the
paths meet. Collision checking is implemented using a 2D
occupancy grid, which is faster and saves memory compared
to 3D explicit mesh collision checking.

Parallelism We leverage parallelism features in Isaac Sim
and Isaac Lab [30, 34] to simulate multiple environments
in parallel per GPU (8 for Pick-and-Place and 2 for Mobile
Manipulation). This scales easily to multiple GPUs in a
cluster. We use NVIDIA L40S GPUs in our experiments.
